_note: Hardscrabble's quests (decision 0350): the main beat, The Thayer Way, and the side quests. Drafts for Matt's friend to rewrite. Voices and facts are in docs/regions/hardscrabble.md; Obed's in docs/briefs/characters/obed-thayer.md. Narration has an empty speaker.

lines.text: There's a gap in the lane's north wall, where the frost has pushed the stones out into the road. The cold is coming through it like a draught under a door.
And something's come through with it.
The stones the frost pushed out lie in the road where they fell.
Back you go, then. All of you.
The stones sit in the gap any which way, rimed white, and the draught stops.
That'll keep the cold out. It won't win any prizes.
Who keeps the walls up here?
Mr. Thayer. Obed Thayer. He walls for nobody, he says.
He'll tell you about it. He's told me.
Who laid the walls along the lane?
Thayers. Four of them, one after another. There's only Obed left.
He walls for nobody. Ask him and he'll tell you about it. Bring a stool.
Who keeps the walls?
Obed Thayer. Out past the end of the street.
He walls for nobody. He'll tell you about it. At length, for him. Four words.
Who mends the walls here?
Mr. Thayer. He walls for nobody. He told me.
He talks to the stones. I talk to the Pikes. Mama says that's different, but it isn't.
Who keeps the walls?
Obed Thayer. He walls for nobody. He'll tell you about it.
He did the low field wall for Truman's father. It's still standing. Everything else is on the wagon.
The man in the yard doesn't look up from the stone he's turning over.
Working.
The patch settles. A stone shifts, then the next, and the whole run of them sinks a finger's width and lies still, like a dog that has turned round twice and lain down.
Obed watches it for a long moment. He says nothing about it.
Your hearting's all at the front. Your throughs don't go through. And it's glued.
Fair.
It isn't. Fair's a word for work.
You'll be Mr. Thayer.
Obed.
There's frost on the hill above the village. It's coming down into the pastures.
Hobble Hill. That's Coyle's wall.
Company bought the hill. The fence man took the old stretch down by the pound and put up his own. Straight as a fence. Mortared.
I told him it'd crack by Christmas.
Did it?
It cracked in a week.
I'm told to keep off the hill. So I keep off it.
The frost is thick up here, and thickest along the top of the hill, where the ring wall runs crooked along the skyline as old walls do.
Except for one stretch, beside the pound. That runs dead straight, squared and grey with mortar, and it's split from end to end. The cold is coming through the cracks.
Oh, that's no good at all.
Inside the pound, something hits the wall. Then again.
The stag goes to Coyle's wall and stands with its nose to the mortar, as if somebody had told it a door would open there.
You want to go home, and the wall won't have you.
I can patch a wall. I can't lay one. Not the way this wants.
I know who can, though. Wait there.
The stag stands at the wall, waiting. It lets Eldwin come close, and doesn't look at him.
I'm fetching him. He'll come. He'll complain, but he'll come.
He's here. He's slow up hills, but he's here.
Obed stands a long time looking at the stag, and the stag looks at the wall.
Hm.
That's not a wall. That's a lid.
He takes his cap off, puts it back on, and starts on Coyle's wall.
He breaks the mortar out with the sledge, a course at a time, throws it down the hill, and sorts the stone into heaps only he understands.
He doesn't hurry, and he doesn't stop.
He lays it again dry, from the footing up. There isn't a trowel of mortar in it.
It doesn't run straight. It goes the way the ground goes, and bends where the stone wants to bend.
Near the middle he sets one stone short and leaves a hand's width open at the bottom, facing north. He doesn't measure it. He doesn't look at it again.
The last stone he turns over twice in his hands. Then he spits on it, and sets it.
There.
The stag walks to the gap and puts its nose down to it, as if it could smell the far side.
Then it goes through, and is gone.
Who set this?
He puts his hand flat on the stone, the way you'd put a hand on a horse, and looks at it for a long time.
That's Thayer work.
That's our work.
Eldwin says nothing.

banner: Hobble Hill and the Long Wall. Put a hand on a lit stone to go to the other.

lines.text: Your patch on the lane. I've not forgotten it.
Come down when you're done looking.
The stone's marks come up out of the cold, lit from inside, and stay lit.

banner: Hobble Hill and the Long Wall. Put a hand on a lit stone to go to the other.

lines.text: The stone is cold. Coyle's mortar has cracked right up against it, and the frost comes through beside it.
Asleep. And no wonder.
The stone is warm under Eldwin's hand. A long way off, another one answers.
The stone is warm under Eldwin's hand. Nothing answers it yet.
That's your patch.
It is.
You made it. You'll unmake it.
He takes the patch down himself, stone by stone, and lays the stones out along the verge, biggest first. The ice in them is already going.
No magic. Hands.
Big ones at the bottom. That one.
It's the size of a loaf, and heavier than it looks.

choice.text: Stand it on its end. It'll fill more of the gap.
Lay it flat, the long side into the wall.
Lay it flat, the long side along the wall.

lines.text: On its end it's a gravestone. Lay it down. Length into the wall.
Eldwin lays it down.
Length in. Right.
It rocks. You've set it on its belly. Turn it over.
Eldwin turns it over. It stops rocking.
Along the face, the first frost walks it out into the road. Length in.
Eldwin turns it.
Now the middle.

choice.text: One big stone. Fewer to set.
Fill it with the small stones.
Leave it hollow. Nobody sees the middle.

lines.text: Then it's a big stone with nothing round it. Hearting. Small stuff.
Eldwin fills the middle with the small stones.
Small stuff first. Always the small stuff first.
Not like seed in a furrow. Pack it. Every one touching.
Eldwin packs it.
The wall sees it.
Eldwin fills it.
That long flat one. That's a through.

choice.text: Lay it along the top, so it looks tidy.
Through, from one face of the wall to the other.
Halfway in. The rest can go in later.

lines.text: Tidy's for curtains. Through. Face to face.
Eldwin puts it through.
Through. Right.
You've got it sloping in. Water runs in, frost follows it. Tip it out.
Eldwin tips it out a hair.
There's no later in a wall. Through.
Eldwin puts it through.
Last course but one. What do you leave?
North. You watched me do it.

choice.text: Nothing. Close it up tight.
A hand's gap, facing south, out of the wind.
A hand's gap, facing north.

lines.text: You've shut it.
Isn't that what a wall is for?
Not that part.
South.
Who told you south?
The wind, I thought.
The wind's not laying this.
Eldwin sets the stone a hand short, and leaves the gap at the bottom, facing north.
Lets it breathe. Don't ask me why. My grandfather didn't know either.
Last stone.
Last stone. You've seen it done.

choice.text: Set it.
Spit on it, then set it.

lines.text: Eldwin lifts it into place. Obed's hand comes down on it before it's set.
You've forgotten something.
Eldwin spits on the last stone, and sets it.
Obed watches him do it with something close to approval.
Fair.
He looks along the patch again.
Nearly.
The wall doesn't settle this time. It doesn't need to.
Obed goes home without another word. That night Eldwin sleeps in the meetinghouse, by the stove, among the empty pews.
What if somebody else paid the postage?
Then it'd be paid. That's all postage wants.
A dozen eggs. I don't take coin. Nobody up here has any, and Patience won't carry it.
The Varnum girl has hens. A great many hens.
Could I have a dozen eggs?
They're the Abbotts' eggs. The Abbotts would want something for them.
What would the Abbotts want?
Something for the Merrills. His leg's bad in the cold. Mama puts a mustard plaster on it, and we've run out.

choice.text: Here. A mustard plaster.
I'll find one.

lines.text: Twelve. I counted them twice. Don't drop any, they're the Abbotts'.
She puts the plaster on the Merrills there and then, and he stands for it.
Mr. Fogg sells them. He sells everything that isn't boots, as well as boots.
Asa counts the eggs, which takes a while, because he counts them twice and then once more for Patience.
Paid. Never had one paid by a stranger.
He gives Eldwin the letter. It's addressed in a careful hand: Obed Thayer, Hardscrabble.
He won't open it with anybody looking. He never opens anything with anybody looking.
Then I won't look.
Eldwin sets the letter on top of the yard wall, and puts a flat stone on it against the wind.
Obed, behind him, looks at the wall and doesn't say anything.
The letter is back on the wall, under its stone. It's been opened, and read, and folded small.

Pa. I'm at the furnace at Furnace Hollow. They feed you and pay in company paper. I laid a firebrick course on the stack Tuesday and the foreman said it was fair work. I thought you'd want to know. Elias.
Eldwin folds it again the way it was, and puts the stone back on it.
The Holts looks at Eldwin, and at the hill, and goes back to what used to be a bonnet.

choice.text: Carry the bonnet up the hill, and let the Holts follow it.
Leave the Holts be.

lines.text: Eldwin carries what's left of the bonnet up the Sheep Walk. The Holts follows it all the way, grumbling, past the wall and into the pound.
Not before the Holts. Sukey was clear about that.
The Pikes bites Eldwin's sleeve, once, to show she could, and then goes up the hill after the Holts.
The Dows leans on Eldwin all the way up the Sheep Walk, which is slower than walking, but she gets there.
The Merrills goes up the hill at a lame horse's pace, with Eldwin's hand on his neck the whole way.
Eldwin herds twelve Abbotts up the Sheep Walk. It takes most of an hour, and he arrives with eleven. The twelfth is already in the pound, waiting.
The Lowells listens to Eldwin explain the plan, then goes up the hill by himself, some other way, and is in the pound first.
Back in the pound, where Sukey says they belong. Nobody seems to mind.
Back in the pound. One of the Abbotts is Eldwin's. She doesn't know it.
You did the Abbotts. All twelve?
All twelve. One of them went ahead.
That's the Abbotts.
You can have a hen. Whichever you like. Not the speckled one.
Would she rather stay with the others?
Yes.
Then I'll leave her where she is, and know she's mine.
That isn't how hens work.
She's yours, though. I'll write it on the barn door.
You wouldn't be going down past the cellar holes?
I might be.
There's a bear sitting in the road down there. He's been at the windfalls in the old dooryards till he's drunk on them.
I want to walk that road south and see the Dows about their boots. Last pair I made them, they'll be through the heels by now. But I'm not walking past a drunk bear.
I'll have a word with him.
A word. Take boots.
The bear's gone off into the birches.
Drunk?
Hiccupping.
Then I'll give him a day to sleep it off, and go.
Here. Stone for your pockets and something for your boots. Don't argue. It goes toward your next resoling.
I'm short of wool for the Shattucks' coat. Good wool. What's left in the village has been through three coats already.
Where would I find a fleece?
Hosea Lamb's down at the pens. He'd spare you one. You found him his forty-third, I hear.
Or Mr. Coyle's sheep on the Sheep Walk are due for shearing. He won't mind. He'll write it down.
Bring me a fleece and I'll show you what I do. The first one's on me.
Could you spare a fleece, for Tamsin Gove?
You fetched her back over the wall. You can have her coat.
He shears the ewe that went over the wall, there and then, in about the time it takes to say so.
She won't miss it till Thursday. Weather's turning, mind.
The sheep looks at Eldwin, decides against him, and trots off up the lane.
He corners her against the wall at the second try. Coyle's shears are hanging on the nearest stake, with a tag on them: COMPANY PROPERTY.
She stands for the shears with the air of somebody who expected worse.
One of the land company's sheep. It looks at Eldwin as if he were a fence.
That'll do. That'll more than do.
She finishes the Shattucks' coat while he watches, talking round the pins in her mouth the whole time.
Now. Something of yours.
No charge for the first. After that I'm as dear as anybody.
The deed to the hill gives its bounds the old way. Listen to this.
'From the heap of stones at the brook, to the split boulder, to the stone with the three marks, and so along the wall as it stands.'
I'd like each mark found and staked, for the ledger. Only the Sheep Walk is full of things that bite, and I'm a land agent.
I'll walk them for you.
At the foot of the walk, where a thread of a brook comes out under the wall, there's a heap of stones, very old and grown over with moss.
The heap of stones at the brook. One.
The boulder is split clean through, as if somebody had laid an axe to it, and a birch is growing in the split.
The split boulder. Two.
Half buried in the turf: a stone with three crossed lines cut in it. Coyle's survey stakes go straight past it, an arm's length off.
The stone with the three marks. Three. You walked right by it, Mr. Coyle.
And so along the wall as it stands. The wall as it stands is Obed's: dry, crooked, with its hand's gap low down, facing north.
As it stands.
The heap at the brook, the split boulder, the three marks. And the wall as it stands.
As it stands.
He reads the deed through. Then he reads it through again.
The wall I took down was in the deed. I took down a bound.
Well. This one's in it now. I'll leave it as it stands.
Mr. Thayer. I'll leave your wall alone.
Hm.
I'll tell Mr. Thayer so myself. I expect he'll say 'Hm.'
Take these. Good boots. I've never once been comfortable in them.

gear.name: Coyle's Good Boots
gear.line: Never comfortable, he says. They walked his bounds.

lines.text: Will you help us load? Once, and properly, and then it's done.
Gladly.
Everything by the door goes on. Don't ask Truman. Truman will have reasons.
A farm wagon, half loaded: a feather bed, a box of crockery, a sack of seed potatoes. There's room on the back for a good deal more.
The wagon. Lucy has put the next thing by the door.

choice.text: Carry out the churn.
Carry out the clock.
Carry out the cradle.
Carry out the chair.
Not yet.

lines.text: Eldwin carries the churn out and sets it on the back of the wagon.
Not the churn. That was my mother's.
It'll get shaken. Butter never comes right in a churn that's been shaken.
He carries it back into the house.
Eldwin carries the clock out, wrapped in a quilt, and lays it in the wagon.
It'll stop on the road. A clock doesn't like a road.
It stops in the house.
It stops in the house when it wants to.
He carries it back in.
Eldwin brings out the cradle. It's small and very old, and the rockers are worn flat underneath.
That was mine. My father's before that.
It'll travel well. It's made to rock.
It's made to stay where it's put.
He takes it in himself.
The last thing by the door is Truman's father's chair. Eldwin carries it out.
When he gets to the wagon, it's nearly empty. The feather bed is gone. So is the crockery.
Lucy is coming back out of the house with nothing in her arms.
She and Truman look at each other over the chair.
Well.
Well.
Truman takes the chair in. Lucy takes the last sack of potatoes. Then Truman goes out to the horse, and unhitches him.
Here. This didn't fit anywhere either.
It's the key to the clock.

gear.name: The Shattucks' Clock Key
gear.line: The clock stays. The key was going to go.

lines.text: A stack of letters on the kitchen shelf, tied with garden twine. They're all addressed the same, and none of them has a stamp or a mark from the post.
Eldwin doesn't touch them.
Those stay where they are.
